{{short description|Migrant children's detention center in Florida, United States}}
{{Use American English|date=September 2025}}
[[File:Homestead Temporary Shelter for Unaccompanied Children.jpg|thumb|Homestead Temporary Shelter for Unaccompanied Children in 2016.]]
'''Homestead Temporary Shelter for Unaccompanied Children''' is a 3,200-bed migrant children's detention center in [[Homestead, Florida]]. Until August 3, 2019, the center had been operated by [[Comprehensive Health Services, Inc.]] (CHSi), which is a subsidiary of the homeland security operator [[Caliburn International]]. It was believed to be the only remaining for-profit child detention center for migrants.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/2019/02/13/694138106/inside-the-largest-and-most-controversial-shelter-for-migrant-children-in-the-u-|title=Inside The Largest And Most Controversial Shelter For Migrant Children In The U.S.|last1=Welch|first1=Leecia|last2=Law|first2=National Center for Youth|website=NPR.org|date=13 February 2019 |language=en|access-date=2019-04-20}}[https://www.yesmagazine.org/people-power/trump-detention-center-children-shut-down-20190905 How We Shut Down the Nation's Largest Child Detention Center], ''[[Yes! (U.S. magazine)|Yes! Magazine]]'', Kristin Kumpf, September 9, 2019.</ref> The organization has faced severe criticism concerning immigration.  Senator [[Elizabeth Warren]] had demanded that the detention facility be "closed down", and calls for investigation and oversight grew stronger when it was revealed that the federal government had paid $33 million in just 46 days for 1,200 of the empty beds.<ref name="Warren">[https://www.newsweek.com/migrant-detention-facility-homestead-florida-taxpayers-immigration-1460180 Trump Administration Must Explain Why U.S. Taxpayers Are Paying 'Outrageous' 'Trump Hotel' Prices to Keep Empty Migrant Detention Center Running: Congressman], ''[[Newsweek]]'', [[Chantal Da Silva|Chantal da Silva]], 9/19/19. Retrieved September 10, 2018.</ref>

It was reported on February 23, 2021 that the administration of [[Joe Biden|US President Joe Biden]] will be reopening the detention center.<ref>{{cite web|last=Cardona|first=Alexi C.|date=Feb 23, 2021|title=Biden to Reopen Homestead Shelter for Immigrant Children|url=https://www.miaminewtimes.com/news/biden-to-reopen-homestead-shelter-for-migrant-children-11881926|website=Miami New Times}}</ref>

== Governance ==

As of September 2019, [[Caliburn International]], a security consulting firm, of which CHS is a subsidiary, faced criticism from south Florida media for its role,<ref name=Warren /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.miaminewtimes.com/news/homestead-miami-child-migrant-camp-contractor-caliburn-cancels-stock-ipo-11105466|title=Homestead Contractor Cancels Stock-Investment Plan After New Times Story, Media /Scrutiny|last=Iannelli|first=Jerry|date=2019-03-05|website=Miami New Times|access-date=2019-04-19}}</ref> particularly because President [[Donald Trump]]'s former [[United States Secretary of Homeland Security|Secretary of Homeland Security]] and [[White House Chief of Staff|Chief of Staff]], General [[John F. Kelly|John Kelly]], sat on the board of and worked as a lobbyist for D.C. Capital Partners (DCCP), before joining the administration in November 2017. DCCP created Caliburn in 2018.<ref name=Warren/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.channele2e.com/business/vertical-markets/caliburn-pursues-ipo-acquisitions/|title=Caliburn Prepares IPO, Pursues IT Services Provider Acquisitions|first=Joe |last=Panettieri|date=2018-12-05|website=ChannelE2E|language=en-US|access-date=2019-04-20}}</ref> Kelly joined Caliburn's Board of Directors after leaving the White House in 2018. He was seen in April 2019 touring the facility on a golf cart.<ref name=nobid/><ref>Monique O. Madan and Ben Wieder {{cite web|url=https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/immigration/article229437719.html|title=Good Friday brings protests, but no apparent changes, at shelter for migrant youths|publisher=Miami Herald|language=en|date=2019-04-19|access-date=2019-04-20}}</ref> Although Caliburn, Comprehensive and DC Capital appear to have accrued financial benefits via government contracts during and subsequent to Kelly's serving as White House chief of staff, legal scholar [[Richard Briffault]] said Kelly did not necessarily break any ethics and conflict of interest rules: "It sounds like he's running between the raindrops. It doesn't sound great, but most likely he's not directly violating any policies." Briffault said government officials are prohibited from benefiting from their involvement in matters involving specific parties. That meant while he served in the White House, Kelly couldn't directly influence any contract-awarding decision to a DC Capital subsidiary. "This is classic revolving door," he continued. That employment meant Kelly couldn't lobby or attempt to influence government policy for five years, although he could return to his former company.<ref name="CBS">{{cite web|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/john-kelly-joins-board-of-caliburn-international-company-operating-largest-unaccompanied-migrant-children-shelter/|title=John Kelly joins board of company operating largest shelter for unaccompanied migrant children|website=www.cbsnews.com|date=3 May 2019 |language=en-US|access-date=2019-05-03}}</ref>

Caliburn's board of directors includes several other retired former [[flag rank]] military personnel including Generals [[Anthony Zinni]] and [[Michael Hayden (general)|Michael Hayden]] and Admirals Stephen F. Loftus, [[Kathleen L. Martin]] and [[James G. Stavridis]]. Other members of the [[military–industrial complex]] on the board include scientist and bureaucrat [[Donald Kerr]] and Ambassadors  [[Michael Corbin]] and decorated U.S. Navy Vietnam veteran and Reagan administration [[United States Assistant Secretary of Defense|Assistant Secretary of Defense]], [[Richard Armitage (naval officer)|Richard Armitage]].<ref name=CBS/> At the end of the Vietnam war, Armitage took a central role in the evacuation of tens of thousands of refugees by sea to the Philippines.<ref>{{cite web|date=September 1, 2010|url=https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=129578263|title=At War's End, U.S. Ship Rescued South Vietnam's Navy|author1=Shapiro, Joseph|author2=Bartlett, Sandra|publisher=NPR|work=[[All Things Considered]]|access-date=December 15, 2019}}</ref> Caliburn's Chief Strategy Officer and Executive Vice President for Corporate Development is retired Vice Admiral [[Frank Craig Pandolfe]].<ref>[https://www.caliburnintl.com/about-caliburn/leadership-team/ Leadership Team - Caliburn International] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190906174708/https://www.caliburnintl.com/about-caliburn/leadership-team/ |date=2019-09-06 }}, ''Caliburn International''. Retrieved October 7, 2017.</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dccapitalpartners.com/pdf/DC_Capital_Fact_Sheet.pdf|title=DC Capital Fact Sheet|website=www.dccapitalpartners.com|language=en-US|access-date=2019-06-26|archive-date=2021-06-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210608204208/http://www.dccapitalpartners.com/pdf/DC_Capital_Fact_Sheet.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=Warren/><ref name=Martin>[https://www.apnews.com/7b9f754aa2fd4a7ba647aebaa98a0693 Private sector seeks to profit by detaining migrant kids], ''[[Associated Press]]'', Garance Burke and Martha Mendoza, October 3, 2019. Retrieved October 4, 2019.</ref>

== Operations ==

The Homestead Temporary Shelter was originally opened during the Obama administration, holding 8,500 juveniles while it operated between June 2016 and April 2017.<ref name="Madan 2019"/><ref name="Madan 2018"/> It was the first in South Florida to be able to house minor immigrants to the [[United States]].<ref name="Hanks 2018">{{cite news|url=https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/community/miami-dade/article213411029.html|title=Up to 1,000 children held by immigration authorities now living in Homestead compound|last1=Hanks|first1=Douglas|date=18 June 2018|work=Miami Herald|access-date=2018-07-02|last2=Medina|first2=Brenda|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.npr.org/2019/01/04/682437566/tent-city-housing-migrant-children-to-close-as-kids-are-released-to-sponsors|title=Tent City Housing Migrant Children To Close As Kids Are Released To Sponsors|work=NPR News|first=John|last=Burnett|date=January 4, 2019|access-date=13 February 2019}}</ref><ref name="Madan 2018">{{cite news|url=https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/immigration/article86137097.html|title=An inside look at what happens to children after crossing the U.S. border|last=Madan|first=Monique O.|date=26 June 2016|work=Miami Herald|access-date=2018-07-02|language=en}}</ref> In 2017, the shelter was shut down when there was no longer a need to house unaccompanied minors, but in early 2018, the shelter was reopened "without public notice."<ref name="Hanks 2018" /> In February 2018, CHSi won a $30 million government contract to run the shelter.<ref name="Iannelli 2018" /> The cost was a million dollars per day.<ref name=vacant>[https://www.yesmagazine.org/people-power/trump-detention-center-children-shut-down-20190905 How We Shut Down the Nation's Largest Child Detention Center], ''[[Yes! (U.S. magazine)|Yes! Magazine]]'', Kristin Kumpf, September 9, 2019.</ref> It was believed that the contract had been crafted in an effort to circumvent the [[Reno v. Flores|Flores Settlement Agreement]] (FSA) which had been arrived at in 1997 after over 11 years of litigation regarding the care of minor immigrants in detention.<ref name=vacant/>

The detention facility is surrounded by tall fencing with security checkpoints in a former [[Job Corps]] building on the [[Homestead Air Reserve Base]].<ref name="Madan 2018" /> Minors in the shelter were provided with meals, snacks, medical care, recreation time and classes.<ref name="Madan 2018" /> The facility was  operated by [[Comprehensive Health Services, Inc.]] (CHSi), used to house minors between the ages of 13 and 17.<ref name="Iannelli 2018">{{cite news|url=http://www.miaminewtimes.com/news/miami-beach-commissioner-threatens-to-punish-child-migrant-facility-contractor-10454554|title=Miami Beach Commissioner Threatens to Ban Child-Migrant Contractor From City Business|last=Iannelli|first=Jerry|date=2018-06-20|work=Miami New Times|access-date=2018-07-02}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.floridatoday.com/story/news/local/2018/06/20/cape-canaveral-detention-center/717375002/|title=Cape Canaveral company runs Homestead facility housing 1,000 migrant children|last=McCarthy|first=John|work=Florida Today|access-date=2018-07-02|language=en}}</ref> Starting in mid-April 2018, CHSi began to advertise to recruit employees to fill about 40 new positions in Homestead.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.abcactionnews.com/news/local-news/i-team-investigates/job-postings-may-shed-light-on-life-for-unaccompanied-migrant-children-at-homestead-shelter|title=Job postings may shed light on life for unaccompanied migrant children at Homestead shelter|last=LaGrone|first=Katie|date=2018-06-22|work=WFTS|access-date=2018-07-02|language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2019, the center became a focal point in the controversy regarding the separating of minor children of asylum seekers at the U.S. Border. On July first and second, a delegation of congressional Democrats visited the facility and raised objections to the conditions in which these minors were kept. The late Maryland Representative [[Elijah Cummings]], who chaired the House Committee on Oversight and Reform, said, "The Trump Administration's actions at the southern border are grotesque and dehumanizing," "There seems to be open contempt for the rule of law and for basic human decency. The Committee needs to hear directly from the heads of these agencies as soon as possible in light of the almost daily reports of abuse and defiance." He invited both acting Secretary [[Kevin McAleenan]] from the [[Department of Homeland Security]] and Acting Commissioner [[Mark Morgan (law enforcement officer)|Mark Morgan]] of the [[U.S. Customs and Border Protection]] at a July 12, 2019 hearing and indicated he would be prepared to subpoena top officials of President [[Donald Trump]]'s administration if they refused his request to testify before the committee. "I encourage Acting Secretary McAleenan and Acting Commissioner Morgan to appear voluntarily in order to answer these critical questions," Cummings indicated that he would subpoena senior Trump officials if they declined his invitation to testify.<ref name=visit>[https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/lawmakers-continue-scrutinize-conditions-immigrant-detention-centers/story?id=64089271 Lawmakers demand change after scrutinizing conditions at immigrant detention centers], ''[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]]'', John Parkinson, July 2, 2019. Retrieved July 3, 2019.</ref> Mississippi Representative [[Bennie Thompson]], who chairs the House Committee on Homeland Security, joined a delegation of Democrats at the detention compound, including Democratic 2020 presidential candidates who visited it while they were in [[Miami, Florida|Miami]] for the Democratic presidential debates that were held on June 26 and 27, 2019.<ref name=visit/>

On July 15, 2019, the center was visited by a congressional delegation which found the government had just rapidly reduced the number of teenagers detained there, a 42% drop in 12 days. Those legislators already intended to analyze how the facility operated and to ask for an accounting for its expenditures. A month earlier, it held 2,460 migrant children, from 13 to 17 years old, an 80% rise since it initially opened in the first quarter of 2018. On July 3, it had held 2,252 children, but by that morning, only 1,309 remained. The chairwoman of the [[United States House Appropriations Subcommittee on Labor, Health and Human Services, Education, and Related Agencies]], Connecticut's [[Rosa DeLauro]], wanted to know if those who had so quickly left had been paired with family members or sponsors, or just transferred to alternate shelters. Congresswoman [[Debbie Wasserman Schultz]], who had previously been refused entry asked, "What the heck. From July 3 until July 14th, suddenly they’re able to drop 1,000 kids here when they couldn’t do that as quickly before? Where did they go?" Caliburn International did not inform them regarding possible closure but did tell them that on July 3, the shelter went on “admittance stop, so no new children have come in since then," and that DHHS began, "...releasing kids as quickly as possible." In the previous week, "448 children were released from the shelter, mostly identified as "reunifications to a sponsor," in addition to transfers to alternate facilities. There were 376 who had been reunified with family and another 70 had been transferred. Two others left because they were over 18 years old. A policy change meant that prior caregivers were no longer required to be fingerprinted.  Deputy Assistant Secretary for public affairs at the DHHS, Mark Weber, described Homestead as "an emergency influx shelter for use when the standard shelter system is near capacity," and space had become available at standard shelters. Miami Congresswoman [[Debbie Mucarsel-Powell]], who had inquired about hurricane planning, said that the lack of such an emergency policy was an "extremely dangerous form of neglect." A Caliburn representative said the facility wasn't accepting new placements and was “not sure for how long” the no-admissions policy would remain.<ref>[https://www.sun-sentinel.com/news/politics/fl-ne-cb-homestead-shelter-detention-center-childen-whereabouts-20190716-6g37kbbaszfx3hdioj7mv2z46u-story.html Where are the 943 migrant children who were moved so quickly from Homestead shelter?], ''South Florida [[Sun Sentinel]]'', Anthony Man, July 16, 2019. Retrieved July 20, 2019.</ref> While most of the minors in the Homestead shelter crossed the border unaccompanied, in June 2018, 94 of the roughly 1,000 children in the center at that time had been separated from their parents at the border under the [[Trump administration family separation policy]].<ref name="Wright 2018">{{cite web|url=https://www.local10.com/news/florida/miami-dade/protesters-gather-outside-homestead-temporary-shelter-for-unaccompanied-children|title=Protesters gather outside Homestead Temporary Shelter for...|last=Wright|first=Madeleine|website=Local 10 News|language=en-US|access-date=2018-07-02|date=2018-06-20}}</ref> Protesters, which included members of the [[American Friends Service Committee]] (AFSC) gathered 128,000 signatures from opponents of the facility.<ref name=vacant/> On June 22, 2018, government officials were allowed to tour the facilities which had 782 boys and 387 girls on the premises.<ref name="Fox 2018">{{cite news|url=http://www.sun-sentinel.com/news/florida/fl-reg-homestead-immigration-tour-20180622-story.html|title=Rubio, journalists tour center for migrant children in Homestead|last=Fox|first=Ben|date=22 June 2018|work=Sun-Sentinel.com|access-date=2018-07-02|language=en-US}}</ref> On average, minors remain in the shelter for around 25 days before they are placed in homes of family or friends who live in the U.S.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://abcnews.go.com/US/reporters-notebook-inside-florida-shelter-immigrant-children/story?id=56090422|title=Reporter's Notebook: Inside a Florida shelter for immigrant children|last=Withers|first=Scott|date=2018-06-22|website=ABC News|language=en|access-date=2018-07-02}}</ref> This is despite current immigration laws that limit detention to only 20 days.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dallasnews.com/news/immigration/2018/09/06/trump-administration-seeks-rule-change-allow-immigrant-children-detained-longer-20-days|title=Trump administration seeks rule change to allow immigrant children to be detained for longer than 20 days|date=2018-09-06|website=Dallas News|language=en|access-date=2019-04-20}}</ref> Despite being contractually obligated to close on April 20, 2019, the facility remained open holding children until August, 2019.<ref name=vacant/><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.tampabay.com/florida-politics/buzz/2018/07/06/miami-republican-barred-from-visiting-immigrant-children-living-in-homestead-compound/|title=Miami Republican barred from visiting immigrant children living in Homestead compound|work=Tampa Bay Times|access-date=December 15, 2019}}</ref> The facility had been opened and closed during the Obama administration and reopened in 2018, and was emptied by August 3, 2019. Its contract was canceled as of November 30, 2019, after being vacant for almost four months.<ref name="Madan 2019">[https://www.miamiherald.com/news/politics-government/article236732048.html Homestead detention center will shut down, but will cost millions to run empty till the end], ''[[Miami Herald]]'', Alex Daughterty and Monique O. Madan, October 28, 2019. Retrieved December 15, 2019.</ref>

== Criticism ==
Protesters opposing the [[Trump administration family separation policy]] demonstrated in front of the Homestead shelter on June 20, 2018.<ref name="Wright 2018" /> The previous day, [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] politicians including, state Representative [[Kionne McGhee]], then-Senator [[Bill Nelson]] and Congresswoman [[Debbie Wasserman Schultz]], were denied entry to the shelter. This led to protesters accusing the Trump administration of trying to cover up mistreatment.<ref name="Fox 2018" /><ref name="Swisher 2018">{{cite news|url=http://www.sun-sentinel.com/news/politics/fl-reg-shelter-inspections-20180628-story.html|title=Watchdog to scrutinize shelters for migrant kids, including 3 in South Florida|last=Swisher|first=Skyler|date=28 June 2018|work=Sun-Sentinel.com|access-date=2018-07-02|language=en-US}}</ref> Senator [[Marco Rubio]] was allowed to visit Homestead on June 22, though he did not describe what he saw.<ref name="Fox 2018" /> In April, 2019, Wasserman Schultz, plus newly elected Congresswomen [[Debbie Mucarsel-Powell]], and [[Donna Shalala]], all representing parts of [[Miami-Dade County]], were refused entry into the facility by the [[United States Department of Health and Human Services|Department of Health and Human Services]] (DHHS), despite their having the legal authority to demand entry.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/immigration/article228933679.html|title=Trump blocks three Florida congresswomen from visiting Homestead child detention center|date=2019-04-09|last=Madan|first=Monique O.|newspaper=Miami Herald|access-date=2019-04-19}}</ref> Shalala headed DHHS for eight years during the Clinton administration.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/former-cabinet-secretary-donna-shalala-to-run-for-congress-in-miami/2018/03/06/a2f6d9ae-215a-11e8-badd-7c9f29a55815_story.html|title=Former Cabinet secretary Donna Shalala to run for Congress in Miami|last1=Scherer|first1=Michael|date=March 6, 2018|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|access-date=July 4, 2019}}</ref> Congressman [[Charlie Crist]], Florida's former governor, termed the situation, "...indefensible. Stunning and disappointing, to say the least." George Sheldon, a former secretary of the [[Florida Department of Children & Families]], characterized the policy as "obscene." "There's no word I can use to describe what I think is an extremely inhumane policy."<ref name=Miller>[https://www.miamiherald.com/news/politics-government/article213525984.html Felony drug defendant tells shocked Miami judge: I work caring for kids seized at border], ''[[Miami Herald]]'', Carol Marbin Miller, June 22, 2018. Retrieved July 5, 2019.</ref>

A protest campaign by local churches, synagogues, and other religious groups has been ongoing since February 20, 2019. Nearly 100 protesters gathered there on April 19, 2019.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/immigration/article229437719.html|title= Good Friday brings protests, but no apparent changes, at shelter for migrant youths|last1=Madan|first1=Monique O.|last2=Wieder|first2=Ben|date=2019-04-19|newspaper=Miami Herald|access-date=2019-04-19}}</ref>

The conditions in which the children were being held were widely criticized including for being regimented and austere. A whistleblower, Andrew Lorentzen-Strait, quit his [[Immigration and Customs Enforcement]] job after 18 years to work in for the private non-profit Lutheran Immigration and Refugee Services. He said, "They say we are the children people, you are the enforcement people, but that is blurred now." "These aren't commodities. They're kids, and they don't need to have big box stores serving them." "You can't just order up migrant care."<ref name=Martin/> In February 2019, reporters on a tour of the facility were informed that older children preferred the huge dormitory holding hundreds of beds, a program manager telling them, "They say it's like a slumber party."<ref name=CBS/>

In [[Topeka, Kansas]], [[Washburn University]] law professor David Rubenstein, whose research is focused on privatized immigrant detention said, "The profiteering incentive comes at the cost of cutting programs or rights or treatment or conditions."<ref name=Martin/>

Two former employees have filed lawsuits claiming they weren't properly trained or paid properly for their work at the shelter. They say that they were hired as travel chaperones but were asked to perform other duties. They claim that their work hours were reduced and then they were fired after complaining about their situation.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.miaminewtimes.com/news/house-oversight-committee-announces-investigation-into-homestead-migrant-shelter-operator-caliburn-international-11217129|title=Employees at Homestead Shelter for Migrant Children Say They Weren't Properly Trained|last1=Shammas|first1=Brittany|date=May 30, 2019|work=[[Miami New Times]]|access-date=July 12, 2019}}</ref>

At a September 18, 2019 hearing of the [[United States House Appropriations Subcommittee on Labor, Health and Human Services, Education, and Related Agencies|U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Health and Human Services, et al.]], in response to a question posed by Representative [[Mark Pocan]], Jonathan Hayes, the acting director of the [[Office of Refugee Resettlement]] said the [[Department of Health and Human Services]] had spent more than $33 million in 46 days to keep the vacant Homestead center in operation although no children were currently housed there. The empty shelter cost taxpayers $720,000 a day: $600 a day for each of 1,200 empty beds at the military base facility. When children are actually present, the cost rises to $750 (~${{Format price|{{Inflation|index=US-GDP|value=750|start_year=2019}}}} in {{Inflation/year|US-GDP}}) daily, per child.<ref>[https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/immigration/article235226457.html Having zero kids at Homestead has cost $33 million so far — that number will rise], ''[[Miami Herald]]'', Monique O. Madan, September 18, 2019. Retrieved September 19, 2019.</ref><ref name=Warren/> Pocan later told ''[[Newsweek]]'' that he felt the explanation Hayes provided was insufficient, and the price being paid would be more than the cost of a "night in the Four Seasons or a Trump hotel." "It's a shocking amount of money to be paying for an empty facility."<ref name=Warren/>
In July 2018, one detainee, a 15-year-old girl from [[Honduras]], escaped from facility workers and was found hiding in a nearby mechanic's shop. Police located her and returned her to the facility. Reports about the incident referred to the facility as a "child prison."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/immigration/article215738665.html|title=Immigrant girl escapes Homestead detention center — and then found hiding in an auto shop|website=miamiherald|language=en|access-date=2019-01-18}}</ref>

In February 2020, [[Eyal Weizman]], Director of [[Forensic Architecture]], was denied entry to the US after being classified as a “security threat” by a Homeland Security algorithm. He had been planning to help launch an investigation into Homestead by teaching local groups Forensic Architecture's research methods into alleged abuses.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pes |first=Javier |date=20 February 2020 |title='It Will Have a Chilling Effect': Forensic Architecture's Eyal Weizman on a Secretive Government Algorithm That Stopped Him Entering the US |url=https://news.artnet.com/art-world/forensic-architecture-algorithm-us-ban-1782441 |access-date=9 May 2025 |website=Artnet News}}</ref>

=== Facility shortcomings ===

A [[Stanford University]] expert in child trauma, Ryan Matlow, expressed concerns that size of the Homestead facility was inappropriate, that it was much too large to address the individual needs of children and that the depersonalization of detainees could produce long term physical and emotional effects, including heart problems and depression. The corporation's plans for additional facilities holding up to 500 children would still be expected to produce such effects.<ref name=Martin/>

The shelter property abuts a military [[Superfund]] site. It is surrounded by soil and groundwater contaminated with dangerous metal and chemicals which include arsenic and lead, and adjacent land was utilized for hazardous waste, munitions, and pesticide storage. Contaminants at such sites can cause a variety of health problems, including being carcinogenic, causing renal failure and developmental damage.<ref name=drawbacks/> Because of chemical contamination, residential development on land surrounding the shelter site is forbidden. An inquiry by the Miami Herald did not disclose any evidence that the shelter site was tested for such contaminants or if it had been evaluated as to their impact on children held there.<ref name=drawbacks/> There was an additional problem regarding exposure to high levels of noise at the center as it is proximate to operations of the Homestead Air Reserve Base's F-16C fighter jets. The center was found to be in a noise zone that according to the United States Air Force (USAF), the [[Federal Aviation Administration]] (FAA) and the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), is "normally unacceptable" for any human residence.<ref name=drawbacks/> According to the World Health Organization (WHO), such a level of sustained noise exposure can be damaging to the cognition and development of children.<ref name=drawbacks>[https://www.miamiherald.com/opinion/op-ed/article235772247.html Potential contamination at Homestead detention center means it can’t be safe to house children], ''[[Miami Herald]]'', Jonathan Fried and Lisa Evans, October 03, 2019. Retrieved December 11, 2019.</ref>

=== Allegations of staff criminality ===
A government watchdog agency, the Office of Inspector General (OIG) for the [[United States Department of Health and Human Services|DHHS]], looked into allegations of [[Sexual abuse|sex abuse]] and extortion in the Homestead shelter.<ref name="Swisher 2018" /> A female worker was charged with attempted coercion and enticement of a recently released minor to engage in illicit sexual activity and attempted production of child pornography.<ref name=Iannelli>{{cite web|url=https://www.miaminewtimes.com/news/five-awful-homestead-miami-child-immigrant-camp-stories-10880065|title=Five Awful Stories About Miami's Child-Migrant Compound|last=Iannelli|first=Jerry|date=2018-11-04|website=Miami New Times|access-date=2019-01-18}}</ref> She was sentenced to ten years in prison.<ref name=Swisher>[https://www.sun-sentinel.com/n/ews/politics/fl-reg-shelter-employee-questions-20180621-story.html From extortion to sex exploitation, South Florida facilities holding migrant kids have faced problems]{{Dead link|date=March 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}, ''South Florida [[Sun-Sentinel]]'', Skyler Swisher, June 22, 2018. Retrieved July 5, 2019.</ref> Questions were raised about background screening. One felon recently hired as a lead worker, had a drug conviction and was currently in drug court when he became employed.<ref name=Swisher/><ref name=Miller/>

=== Contractor favoritism ===

In December 2016, Comprehensive Health Services (CHSi) announced a new project that would "create 150 new jobs" at its Cape Canaveral headquarters. Consequently, in July 2017, the state awarded it a $600,000 (~${{Format price|{{Inflation|index=US-GDP|value=600000|start_year=2017}}}} in {{Inflation/year|US-GDP}}) "qualified target-industry" tax-incentive package. As then-Governor, now-U.S. Senator [[Rick Scott]] negotiated that tax break, Comprehensive Health concluded a deal to pay a $3.8 million settlement to the U.S. Department of Justice to settle a medical-fraud claim. The corporation paid the fine in February 2017, without admitting guilt, but the state of Florida still issued the tax breaks.<ref name=Iannelli/> Despite an absence of competitive bidding, in late April 2019, CHSi was granted a new contract worth at least $341 million, but which could increase substantially if the population of children continued to rise.<ref name=nobid>[https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/immigration/article229744049.html Critics deplore this migrant shelter. Its operator just got a huge, hush-hush no-bid deal], ''[[Miami Herald]]'', Monique O. Madan, May 1, 2019. Retrieved July 5, 2019.</ref> A joint investigation by the [[Associated Press]] and the PBS investigative journalism flagship feature, [[Frontline (American TV program)|Frontline]], found that although the shelter had been completely empty for two months, it still had 2,000 staff on hand.<ref name=Martin/> There had been concerted initiatives on the part of the Trump administration to shift detained children from non-profit, often religious denomination-operated shelters, to Caliburn and other for-profit prison operators, such as the [[GEO Group]]. Trump's [[Health and Human Services]] Secretary, a long time Republican executive and judicial branch insider, [[Alex Azar]],<ref name="whois">{{cite news |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/2017/11/13/former-pharmaceutical-ceo-nominated-trump-head-department-health-and-human-services/858240001/|title=Who is Alex Azar? Former drugmaker CEO and HHS official nominated to head agency |last=Groppe |first=Maureen |date=November 13, 2017|work=[[USA Today]]|access-date=October 6, 2019}}</ref> called the findings of the investigators "misleading," but avoided addressing the shifting to for-profit privatization providers, which were exclusive to Caliburn at the time. Six other Comprehensive Health Services programs in Texas that were holding migrant children were booming, including those in [[San Benito, Texas|San Benito]], [[Brownsville, Texas|Brownsville]], and [[Los Fresnos, Texas|Los Fresnos]]. In early June, CHSi had been holding almost 25% of all the migrant children who were in custody at that time.<ref name=Martin/> The corporation had received almost $300 million in 2019 when the story was written.<ref name=Martin/><ref name=Burke>[https://www.apnews.com/7b9f754aa2fd4a7ba647aebaa98a0693 Private sector seeks to profit by detaining migrant kids], ''[[Associated Press]]'', Garance Burke and Martha Mendoza, October 3, 2019. Retrieved October 6, 2019.</ref>
